summary.text: Physiology is the scientific study of the functions and mechanisms of living systems.
It asks how organisms, organ systems, organs, cells and biomolecules carry out chemical and physical functions, relying on homeostatic control and communication between cells.
It draws on anatomy, biochemistry, biophysics, genetics and evolutionary biology, and it is studied alongside anatomy because structure and function often dictate one another.

items.prompt: A researcher records two hearts: one in a healthy runner and one in a patient with heart disease. What does physiology call the healthy runner's condition?

options.label: A pathological state, meaning abnormal conditions
A physiological state, meaning normal function
A comparative state, meaning cross-species diversity
A cellular state, meaning one cell's activity

items.explain: A physiological state is the condition of normal function, while a pathological state refers to abnormal conditions such as human diseases.

items.prompt: Why are medical students taught what organs look like alongside how they work?

options.label: Organ shapes never change, so function can be learned apart
Function is only about chemistry, so shape hardly matters
Structure and function are often dictated by each other
Function can be read directly from an organ's name

items.explain: Because form and function are often connected, physiology and anatomy are linked and studied in tandem.

items.prompt: Which everyday scene is an example of plant physiology at work?

options.label: A botanist labelling a leaf by its shape
A gardener counting the petals on a flower
A museum cataloguing pressed leaves by name
A seedling's shoot growing toward a sunny window

items.explain: Growth of shoots towards light is one of the examples of plant physiology, since it is about how a plant functions.

items.prompt: A scientist asks how animals sense light, sound and temperature while keeping a stable internal environment. Which field helps explain this?

options.label: Biophysics, the study of physical properties of living things
Genetics, the study of heredity and trait variation
Anatomy, the study of structure and organization
Biochemistry, the study of chemical processes in organisms

items.explain: Biophysics studies the physical properties of organisms and helps explain how they sense stimuli and maintain homeostasis.

items.prompt: After a patient starts a new medication, her behavior changes noticeably. How might doctors use that change?

options.label: As proof the medication has no effect on her body
As a clue to her health, since physiology can affect the mind
As a sign her four humors have separated
As a direct measure of how her organs are built

items.explain: Changes in physiology can affect mental functions, and behavior change from such substances is often used to assess the health of individuals.

items.prompt: Early Greek writers such as Hippocrates and Aristotle leaned on theories like the four humors. Who was the first to run experiments to probe how the body functions?

options.label: Hippocrates, in the late 5th century BC
Aristotle, who stressed structure and function
Galen, who lived around 130 to 200 AD
Nobody; experiments came only in modern times

items.explain: Galen was the first to use experiments to probe the functions of the body.

paragraphs.heading: What physiology studies
paragraphs.text: Physiology is the science of how living systems function, named from Greek words for "nature" and "study". It asks how whole organisms, organ systems, single organs, cells and biomolecules carry out chemical and physical work. At its heart are biophysical and biochemical processes, homeostatic control, and communication between cells. Homeostasis means keeping a stable internal environment.

paragraphs.heading: Normal and abnormal
paragraphs.text: The physiological state is the condition of normal function, while the pathological state covers abnormal conditions, including human diseases. The field can be split by the kind of organism studied into medical, animal, plant, cell and comparative physiology. Much of what is known about human physiology was built on experiments with animals.

paragraphs.heading: Neighbouring sciences
paragraphs.text: Physiology leans on several other fields. Anatomy, the study of structure from cells and tissues up to organs, matters because structure and function often dictate each other, which is why the two are studied together in medical training. Biochemistry explains the chemical processes underneath cell and molecular life, and biophysics explains how organisms sense and respond to light, sound and temperature. Genetics shows how genes and the environment shape an organism's traits, and evolutionary biology explains where physiological processes came from and why they help organisms cope.

paragraphs.heading: Cells and plants
paragraphs.text: Animal, plant and microbial cells differ, but the basic work of any cell comes down to division, signalling, growth and metabolism. Plant physiology, a branch of botany, studies how plants function, from photosynthesis and respiration to nutrition, circadian rhythms, seed germination and dormancy. Roots soaking up water, leaves making food and shoots growing toward light are all examples.

paragraphs.heading: The human body
paragraphs.text: Human physiology studies how the body's systems work together to hold a stable internal environment. It covers the nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive and urinary systems, along with cell and exercise physiology. The endocrine and nervous systems play major roles in receiving and sending the signals that tie the body's functions together, through both electrical and chemical communication. Understanding all this is essential for diagnosing and treating health conditions.

paragraphs.heading: Ancient beginnings
paragraphs.text: Human physiology as a medical field began in classical Greece, around the time of Hippocrates in the late 5th century BC, and early forms seem to have existed then in China, India and elsewhere too. Hippocrates used the theory of four humors: black bile, phlegm, blood and yellow bile. Aristotle's focus on how structure relates to function marked the start of physiology in Ancient Greece. Later, Galen, who lived around 130–200 AD, was the first to test how the body works by experiment.
